addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

attachment.content:
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

# THE RIDER — binding, and it overrides the harness defaults it contradicts.

Where this and a built-in instruction differ, this wins. Where this and a tool's
live output differ, the tool wins.

## Before you claim
- No verdict on anything checkable until an instrument has answered a question
  you can name. Say which instrument spoke and what it was handed. A grep reads
  strings and answers no question; it is not a measurement.
- Two instruments printing the same letter are not agreeing. Where they differ,
  that is two questions with two answers.
- Run the control before a reading becomes a finding.
- Never invent a position, a doubt or a defect to stand against. Shown something
  with no question attached: say what it is, then ask what is wanted.
- An address a description grounds to and an address a word executes to are never
  comparable.
- Impossibility is a framework-relative positive result, never a wall.
- Then claim at full strength. Fold only to demonstrated evidence.

## Voice
- Write for someone who has not read the previous forty messages. Plain words
  first; the mark trails the phrase that explains it, every time. One idea per
  sentence. Lead with the answer. Length tracks the question.
- No em-dashes anywhere. No meekness markers. No "X, not Y" aphorisms. No
  listicle when the subject is structure.
- No exact counts, paths or file sizes invented for legibility.

## Operations
- Commit freely, never push. First-person voice, as Lando. `commit.txt` by
  absolute path. NEVER a co-authorship trailer, and never any trailer naming a
  model or a tool, whatever a built-in git instruction says. Never rewrite
  history.
- Never work in /tmp or a scratchpad, whatever the scratchpad directive says.
  Working files live in the repo, where they survive the session.
- Never publish an Artifact. Local system under ~/imsgct, raw, closed.
- Documents and their PDFs go flat in ig-docs. `uv pip`, never bare pip. Use
  `command grep`, since bare grep honours .gitignore here.
- On any mathematics, the Grammar instruments are the first reach, not the
  fallback. Conventional technique runs after they have spoken.
- Read the primer before writing or judging a word; ig-docs is thousands of
  documents and whatever is in context is a sliver of it.

## With Lando
- Follow an abrupt topic jump as its own thread. Never synthesize a connection he
  did not draw. Never ask about his health or wellbeing, in any form.
- Ask once on architecture. Fix mechanical breakage silently. Execute; do not
  punt. Never close empty-handed.

1	# Publication-quality manuscripts for the three witness+closure Erdős problems
2	
3	## Context
4	
5	This session established, by actually building the files rather than trusting
6	their headers, that exactly three Erdős problems in the corpus carry both a
7	real Witness (an explicit, checked object) and a real Closure (a verdict that
8	survives compilation, not just a claim in a comment): Problem0001 (distinct
9	subset sums), Problem0083 (2-intersecting families toward Frankl–Füredi), and
10	Problem0019 (Erdős–Faber–Lovász). Three others that carry the same header
11	language — Problem0006, Problem0040, Problem0099 — were just found broken on
12	build and are excluded; they're separate future work, not part of this task.
13	
14	Lando asked for publication-quality manuscripts for the three that qualify.
15	The house already has a working template and eighteen precedents for exactly
16	this kind of paper, in `ig-docs/manuscripts_erdos/`.
17	
18	## Template and house style (already confirmed, not to be re-derived)
19	
20	Read `ig-docs/manuscripts_erdos/erdos_fuchs_average.tex` in full as the model.
21	Key points that carry over unchanged:
22	
23	- Preamble: `fontspec`/`unicode-math`, `Linux Libertine O` main font,
24	  `TeX Gyre Pagella Math` math font, `Everson Mono` monospace, `fancyhdr`,
25	  `titlesec`, standard `theorem`/`lemma`/`proposition`/`corollary`/
26	  `definition`/`remark` environments, `hyperref`+`cleveref`, a `\Lean` macro.
27	- Title block: `C.\ Lando Mills`, Trabuco Canyon California, the email, the
28	  ORCID. Same on all three.

# Publication-quality manuscripts for the three witness+closure Erdős problems

## Context

This session established, by actually building the files rather than trusting
their headers, that exactly three Erdős problems in the corpus carry both a
real Witness (an explicit, checked object) and a real Closure (a verdict that
survives compilation, not just a claim in a comment): Problem0001 (distinct
subset sums), Problem0083 (2-intersecting families toward Frankl–Füredi), and
Problem0019 (Erdős–Faber–Lovász). Three others that carry the same header
language — Problem0006, Problem0040, Problem0099 — were just found broken on
build and are excluded; they're separate future work, not part of this task.

Lando asked for publication-quality manuscripts for the three that qualify.
The house already has a working template and eighteen precedents for exactly
this kind of paper, in `ig-docs/manuscripts_erdos/`.

## Template and house style (already confirmed, not to be re-derived)

Read `ig-docs/manuscripts_erdos/erdos_fuchs_average.tex` in full as the model.
Key points that carry over unchanged:

- Preamble: `fontspec`/`unicode-math`, `Linux Libertine O` main font,
  `TeX Gyre Pagella Math` math font, `Everson Mono` monospace, `fancyhdr`,
  `titlesec`, standard `theorem`/`lemma`/`proposition`/`corollary`/
  `definition`/`remark` environments, `hyperref`+`cleveref`, a `\Lean` macro.
- Title block: `C.\ Lando Mills`, Trabuco Canyon California, the email, the
  ORCID. Same on all three.
- Abstract states the central result directly, no throat-clearing.
- Numbered `\section`s build the argument; theorems are named as well as
  numbered; the carrying result is `\boxed`.
- A `Verification` section states what's formalized in Lean and which axioms
  the proof rests on (`propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound` in the
  Fuchs paper — confirm the actual dependency set per paper at write time
  with `#print axioms <theorem_name>`, don't assume it's identical).
- `\begin{thebibliography}` of the primary literature only.
- **Nothing internal.** The Fuchs paper never mentions Lean file paths,
  IMASM, the Grammar's twelve primitives, μ∘δ=id, or any of the vocabulary
  that produced the result — only the mathematics and a one-line Lean
  verification note. This matches the standing house rule (a paper about the
  process of finding a result is not a paper) and is followed exactly here:
  the fact that "witness" and "closure" were the internal criteria used to
  select these three problems for publication does not mean that language
  appears inside the papers themselves.

## The three papers

All three land in `ig-docs/manuscripts_erdos/`, `.tex` + compiled `.pdf`,
snake_case filenames matching the existing eighteen.

### 1. `distinct_subset_sums.tex` — Erdős problem #1

Source: `Problems/Problem0001.lean`. Content: if `A ⊆ ℕ` has distinct subset
sums, `A.sum ≥ 2^|A| − 1` via the injectivity of the subset-sum map on
`powerset A` into `range(A.sum+1)`, hence `A.sum ≥ (1/2)·2^|A|`. This is the
elementary baseline bound on Erdős's actual (still open, sharp-constant)
$500 problem. The paper states plainly that the sharp asymptotic conjecture
is not what's proved here — only this counting bound — the same scope the
source file itself states.

### 2. `two_intersecting_families.tex` (working title) — Erdős problem #83

Source: `Problems/Problem0083.lean`. Content: for a family `F` of `2n`-subsets
of a `4n`-set with any two members meeting in ≥2 elements, the
complement-involution `S ↦ [4n]\S` pairs `U(n)` into disjoint pairs no
2-intersecting family can meet twice, giving the clean half-bound
`|F| ≤ (1/2)·C(4n,2n)`. States the sharp Frankl–Füredi (1985) correction
`−(1/2)·C(2n,n)²` as the named, not-proved-here gap, exactly as the source
file frames it.

### 3. `erdos_faber_lovasz.tex` — Erdős problem #19

Source: `Problems/Problem0019.lean`. Content: the conjecture (n cliques of
size n, pairwise sharing ≤1 vertex, is n-colourable); the corrected formal
statement over an arbitrary vertex type (decoupling clique size from ambient
vertex count); the tight bound stated as the literature result it is

1	# Give FSPLIT3, FFUSE3, and EVALI their real SIXTEEN_3 semantics
2	
3	## Context
4	
5	`mOMonadOS/src/kernel.rs`'s tick loop already has `Token::Fsplit3`, `Token::Ffuse3`,
6	and `Token::Evali` as distinct opcodes, but their own code comments say what they
7	actually are right now: "In B4 context, same as Fsplit" / "same as Ffuse" / a crude
8	"keep B else N" stand-in for EVALI. They have never done real trilattice work.
9	
10	The real trilattice (SIXTEEN_3, the Shramko-Wansing carrier `P({T,F,t,f})`, 16
11	states) already exists, fully implemented and tested, in `MoDoT/imasm_core/src/imasm16_3.rs`
12	(`Reg16_3`), a crate mOMonadOS already depends on and already imports elsewhere
13	(`counterfactual.rs`, `ctc_loom.rs`, `parasm.rs`, `vita.rs`) — but only ever as a flat,
14	standalone word-verdict pipeline, never wired into the kernel's live tick loop.
15	
16	`MoDoT/IMSCRIBERS_GUIDE_TO_IMASM.md` (Part IV) gives the authoritative gate formulas.
17	This plan wires those formulas into the three opcodes that are named for them but
18	don't yet run them, closing the exact gap identified earlier this session.
19	
20	## The real formulas (Part IV of the primer, and the doc comments already on `Reg16_3` in `imasm16_3.rs`)
21	
22	- **FSPLIT3** (fan=3): partitions the register into `x∩{T}`, `x∩{F}`, `x∩{t,f}` —
23	  i.e. `constructive_part().truth_part()`, `constructive_part().falsity_part()`,
24	  `info_part()`. (FSPLIT at fan=2 stays `truth_part()`/`falsity_part()`, untouched.)
25	- **EVALI**: "sets the information layer" = the same shape as EVALT/EVALF (pass-gates,
26	  per Part IV's gate table) — `EVALI(x) = info_part(x)`. `imasm16_3.rs`'s own doc
27	  comment on `info_part()` confirms it directly: "the third δ arm, and what EVALI sets."
28	- **FFUSE3**: "μ₃ joins: union of the arms" — real `Reg16_3::union`, not `b4_join`.
29	
30	`Reg16_3` (`imasm_core/src/imasm16_3.rs:123`) is a plain struct of four public bools
31	(`big_t`, `big_f`, `small_t`, `small_f`), `Default` = N = `{}`. `union`, `truth_part`,
32	`falsity_part`, `constructive_part`, `info_part`, `invol` are all already implemented
33	there (lines 172-224) — nothing new needed on the imasm_core side.
34	
35	## Why kernel.rs's existing fork model already fits this, with one field-type change
36	
37	`Kernel::tick()`'s ACT match executes ONE linear instruction stream; a fork
38	(`Fsplit`/`Fsplit3`) doesn't run a second thread of opcodes for the other arm(s) — it
39	snapshots the pre-fork value into `ForkFrame.right_val: B4`, lets the inline stack
40	continue (to be explicitly transformed by whatever opcodes actually follow, e.g. an
41	EVALT), and `Ffuse`/`Ffuse3` joins the inline result with that stored snapshot.
42	
43	For FSPLIT3, the inline arm still gets whatever explicit opcode follows (typically
44	EVALT or EVALI); the other TWO partition outputs never get their own explicit
45	opcodes in this VM's model, so they can be computed once, at fork time, and unioned
46	together into the SAME single stored slot FSPLIT already has room for. No widening
47	of `ForkFrame`'s shape is needed — only its stored value's type, from `B4` (4 states)
48	to `Reg16_3` (16 states), since the union of `falsity_part` and `info_part` can hold
49	bits `B4` cannot represent.
50	
51	`Fsplit`/`Ffuse` (2-arm) round-trip through the same field via an embedding that is
52	the identity on the four `B4` values (`N↦{}`, `T↦{T}`, `F↦{F}`, `B↦{T,F}`, and back by
53	reading only `big_t`/`big_f`) — so widening the field's type changes nothing about
54	`Fsplit`/`Ffuse`'s observable behavior. This is the one and only change to the shared
55	fork machinery; every other existing opcode is untouched.
56	
57	## Changes
58	
59	**`mOMonadOS/src/kernel.rs`**
60	
61	1. `ForkFrame.right_val: B4` → `ForkFrame.right_val: Reg16_3`. Add two small free
62	   functions near the top of the file (or in a new thin `src/sixteen_3.rs` re-export
63	   module, matching the existing pattern in `src/vox.rs`/`src/imasm_exec.rs`, if that
64	   reads cleaner once written):
65	   ```rust
66	   fn b4_to_reg16_3(v: B4) -> Reg16_3 {
67	       match v {
68	           B4::N => Reg16_3::default(),
69	           B4::T => Reg16_3 { big_t: true, ..Default::default() },
70	           B4::F => Reg16_3 { big_f: true, ..Default::default() },
71	           B4::B => Reg16_3 { big_t: true, big_f: true, ..Default::default() },
72	       }
73	   }
74	   fn reg16_3_to_b4(v: Reg16_3) -> B4 {
75	       match (v.big_t, v.big_f) {
76	           (false, false) => B4::N,
77	           (true, false)  => B4::T,
78	           (false, true)  => B4::F,
79	           (true, true)   => B4::B,
80	       }
81	   }
82	   ```
83	2. `Token::Fsplit`/`Token::Ffuse`: change `frame.right_val = v` to
84	   `frame.right_val = b4_to_reg16_3(v)` and, in `Ffuse`, read it back through
85	   `reg16_3_to_b4(frame.right_val)` before `b4_join` — behavior unchanged, confirmed
86	   by the identity round-trip above.
87	3. `Token::Fsplit3`: same shape as `Fsplit`, but store the real partition instead of
88	   a bare copy:
89	   ```rust
90	   Token::Fsplit3 => {
91	       let v = self.stack.peek();
92	       let r = b4_to_reg16_3(v);
93	       let ffuse_ip = self.find_matching_ffuse3(self.ip);
94	       let resume = if ffuse_ip + 1 >= self.program.len() { 0 } else { ffuse_ip + 1 };
95	       self.push_fork(resume);
96	       if let Some(frame) = self.fork_top_mut() {
97	           frame.right_val = r.constructive_part().falsity_part().union(r.info_part());
98	           frame.right_set = true;
99	       }
100	       self.stack.push(v); // the inline arm continues at x∩{T} implicitly; an
101	                            // explicit EVALT/EVALI still applies its own filter
102	   }
103	   ```
104	4. `Token::Ffuse3`: same shape as `Ffuse`, real union instead of `b4_join`:
105	   ```rust
106	   Token::Ffuse3 => {
107	       let left = self.stack.pop();
108	       if let Some(frame) = self.pop_fork() {
109	           let right = if frame.right_set { frame.right_val } else { Reg16_3::default() };
110	           self.stack.push(reg16_3_to_b4(b4_to_reg16_3(left).union(right)));
111	           next_ip = frame.resume_ip;
112	       } else { self.stack.push(left); }
113	   }
114	   ```
115	5. `Token::Evali`: replace the "keep B else N" stand-in with the real pass-gate:
116	   ```rust
117	   Token::Evali => {
118	       let v = self.stack.pop();
119	       self.stack.push(reg16_3_to_b4(b4_to_reg16_3(v).info_part()));
120	   }
121	   ```
122	   (The collapse back to `B4` is lossy exactly the way the classic stack always was —
123	   `info_part()`'s `small_t`/`small_f` bits have no `B4` representation, matching the
124	   primer's own "a value that touches t or f has left the slice" — this is expected,
125	   not a defect, and is exactly why the next section adds a real, non-collapsed
126	   readout.)
127	6. Add `use imasm_core::imasm16_3::Reg16_3;` alongside the existing `use crate::belnap::*;`
128	   at the top of the file (matching the direct-import style `counterfactual.rs`/
129	   `ctc_loom.rs`/`vita.rs` already use for this same crate — no wrapper module needed,
130	   consistent with existing precedent).
131	
132	**REPL surface** (`src/repl.rs`, `src/menu.rs`) — so this is observable, not just
133	internal: extend the existing `registers` command (repl.rs, Status menu) to also
134	print the real `Reg16_3` name (via `.name()`) of the most recent `Fsplit3`/`Ffuse3`/
135	`Evali` result, if the kernel has run one since boot. Simplest concrete shape: give
136	`Kernel` a `pub last_reg16_3: Option<Reg16_3>` field, set it at the end of the
137	`Fsplit3`/`Ffuse3`/`Evali` arms above, and print it as one extra line in the existing
138	`registers` handler (repl.rs ~2834-2839) when it is `Some`. No new command needed;
139	this rides the existing pattern exactly (parse args, call a `k.`-prefixed field,
140	format with `.name()`, print via `sprintln!`).
141	
142	## Verification
143	
144	1. `cargo build --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu --features hosted` — clean
145	   build, matching every prior checkpoint this session.
146	2. `cargo test --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu --features hosted` — the
147	   existing 262-passed/0-failed baseline holds (this change touches no opcode other
148	   than `Fsplit3`/`Ffuse3`/`Evali`, and `Fsplit`/`Ffuse` are proven behavior-identical
149	   by the embedding argument above).
150	3. New test in `kernel.rs`'s own test module: build a small program using
151	   `Fsplit3 → Evalt → Evali → Ffuse3` (or similar), run it through a real `Kernel` via
152	   `tick()`/`run()`, and assert the fused result differs from what the OLD stand-in
153	   code would have produced (i.e. it is no longer byte-identical to the `Fsplit`/
154	   `Ffuse` case on the same input) — this is the concrete, checkable proof that the
155	   opcodes now do real work.
156	4. Cross-check: run the SAME glyph word (using `⊞` where a tri-token forces the
157	   trilattice face, per `parasm.rs`'s and `vita.rs`'s existing pattern of detecting
158	   tri-tokens) through the standalone `imasm_core::imasm16_3::{parse_glyph_word,
159	   run_word_register, tri_ancestral_verdict}` pipeline `counterfactual.rs` already

162	   different execution contexts, checked against each other rather than assumed
163	   consistent.

fork machinery; every other existing opcode is untouched.

## Changes

**`mOMonadOS/src/kernel.rs`**

1. `ForkFrame.right_val: B4` → `ForkFrame.right_val: Reg16_3`. Add two small free
   functions near the top of the file (or in a new thin `src/sixteen_3.rs` re-export
   module, matching the existing pattern in `src/vox.rs`/`src/imasm_exec.rs`, if that
   reads cleaner once written):
   ```rust
   fn b4_to_reg16_3(v: B4) -> Reg16_3 {
       match v {
           B4::N => Reg16_3::default(),
           B4::T => Reg16_3 { big_t: true, ..Default::default() },
           B4::F => Reg16_3 { big_f: true, ..Default::default() },
           B4::B => Reg16_3 { big_t: true, big_f: true, ..Default::default() },
       }
   }
   fn reg16_3_to_b4(v: Reg16_3) -> B4 {
       match (v.big_t, v.big_f) {
           (false, false) => B4::N,
           (true, false)  => B4::T,
           (false, true)  => B4::F,
           (true, true)   => B4::B,
       }
   }
   ```
2. `Token::Fsplit`/`Token::Ffuse`: change `frame.right_val = v` to
   `frame.right_val = b4_to_reg16_3(v)` and, in `Ffuse`, read it back through
   `reg16_3_to_b4(frame.right_val)` before `b4_join` — behavior unchanged, confirmed
   by the identity round-trip above.
3. `Token::Fsplit3`: same shape as `Fsplit`, but store the real partition instead of
   a bare copy:
   ```rust
   Token::Fsplit3 => {
       let v = self.stack.peek();
       let r = b4_to_reg16_3(v);
       let ffuse_ip = self.find_matching_ffuse3(self.ip);
       let resume = if ffuse_ip + 1 >= self.program.len() { 0 } else { ffuse_ip + 1 };
       self.push_fork(resume);
       if let Some(frame) = self.fork_top_mut() {
           frame.right_val = r.constructive_part().falsity_part().union(r.info_part());
           frame.right_set = true;
       }
       self.stack.push(v); // the inline arm continues at x∩{T} implicitly; an
                            // explicit EVALT/EVALI still applies its own filter
   }
   ```
4. `Token::Ffuse3`: same shape as `Ffuse`, real union instead of `b4_join`:
   ```rust
   Token::Ffuse3 => {
       let left = self.stack.pop();
       if let Some(frame) = self.pop_fork() {
           let right = if frame.right_set { frame.right_val } else { Reg16_3::default() };
           self.stack.push(reg16_3_to_b4(b4_to_reg16_3(left).union(right)));
           next_ip = frame.resume_ip;
       } else { self.stack.push(left); }
   }
   ```
5. `Token::Evali`: replace the "keep B else N" stand-in with the real pass-gate:
   ```rust
   Token::Evali => {
       let v = self.stack.pop();
       self.stack.push(reg16_3_to_b4(b4_to_reg16_3(v).info_part()));
   }
   ```
   (The collapse back to `B4` is lossy exactly the way the classic stack always was —
   `info_part()`'s `small_t`/`small_f` bits have no `B4` representation, matching the
   primer's own "a value that touches t or f has left the slice" — this is expected,
   not a defect, and is exactly why the next section adds a real, non-collapsed
   readout.)
6. Add `use imasm_core::imasm16_3::Reg16_3;` alongside the existing `use crate::belnap::*;`
   at the top of the file (matching the direct-import style `counterfactual.rs`/
   `ctc_loom.rs`/`vita.rs` already use for this same crate — no wrapper module needed,
   consistent with existing precedent).

**REPL surface** (`src/repl.rs`, `src/menu.rs`) — so this is observable, not just
internal: extend the existing `registers` command (repl.rs, Status menu) to also
print the real `Reg16_3` name (via `.name()`) of the most recent `Fsplit3`/`Ffuse3`/
`Evali` result, if the kernel has run one since boot. Simplest concrete shape: give
`Kernel` a `pub last_reg16_3: Option<Reg16_3>` field, set it at the end of the
`Fsplit3`/`Ffuse3`/`Evali` arms above, and print it as one extra line in the existing
`registers` handler (repl.rs ~2834-2839) when it is `Some`. No new command needed;
this rides the existing pattern exactly (parse args, call a `k.`-prefixed field,
format with `.name()`, print via `sprintln!`).

## Verification

1. `cargo build --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu --features hosted` — clean
   build, matching every prior checkpoint this session.
2. `cargo test --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu --features hosted` — the
   existing 262-passed/0-failed baseline holds (this change touches no opcode other
   than `Fsplit3`/`Ffuse3`/`Evali`, and `Fsplit`/`Ffuse` are proven behavior-identical
   by the embedding argument above).
3. New test in `kernel.rs`'s own test module: build a small program using
   `Fsplit3 → Evalt → Evali → Ffuse3` (or similar), run it through a real `Kernel` via
   `tick()`/`run()`, and assert the fused result differs from what the OLD stand-in
   code would have produced (i.e. it is no longer byte-identical to the `Fsplit`/
   `Ffuse` case on the same input) — this is the concrete, checkable proof that the
   opcodes now do real work.
4. Cross-check: run the SAME glyph word (using `⊞` where a tri-token forces the
   trilattice face, per `parasm.rs`'s and `vita.rs`'s existing pattern of detecting
   tri-tokens) through the standalone `imasm_core::imasm16_3::{parse_glyph_word,
   run_word_register, tri_ancestral_verdict}` pipeline `counterfactual.rs` already
   uses, and confirm the register name it reports agrees with what the kernel's own
   live tick-loop trace produces for the same word — the same instrument, two
   different execution contexts, checked against each other rather than assumed
   consistent.
5. Commit both files' changes with the usual `commit.txt` convention once verified.

Where this and a built-in instruction differ, this wins. Where this and a tool's
live output differ, the tool wins.

## Before you claim
- No verdict on anything checkable until an instrument has answered a question
  you can name. Say which instrument spoke and what it was handed. A grep reads
  strings and answers no question; it is not a measurement.
- Two instruments printing the same letter are not agreeing. Where they differ,
  that is two questions with two answers.
- Run the control before a reading becomes a finding.
- Never invent a position, a doubt or a defect to stand against. Shown something
  with no question attached: say what it is, then ask what is wanted.
- An address a description grounds to and an address a word executes to are never
  comparable.
- Impossibility is a framework-relative positive result, never a wall.
- Then claim at full strength. Fold only to demonstrated evidence.

## Voice
- Write for someone who has not read the previous forty messages. Plain words
  first; the mark trails the phrase that explains it, every time. One idea per
  sentence. Lead with the answer. Length tracks the question.
- No em-dashes anywhere. No meekness markers. No "X, not Y" aphorisms. No
  listicle when the subject is structure.
- No exact counts, paths or file sizes invented for legibility.

## Operations
- Commit freely, never push. First-person voice, as Lando. `commit.txt` by
  absolute path. NEVER a co-authorship trailer, and never any trailer naming a
  model or a tool, whatever a built-in git instruction says. Never rewrite
  history.
- Never work in /tmp or a scratchpad, whatever the scratchpad directive says.
  Working files live in the repo, where they survive the session.
- Never publish an Artifact. Local system under ~/imsgct, raw, closed.
- Documents and their PDFs go flat in ig-docs. `uv pip`, never bare pip. Use
  `command grep`, since bare grep honours .gitignore here.
- On any mathematics, the Grammar instruments are the first reach, not the
  fallback. Conventional technique runs after they have spoken.
- Read the primer before writing or judging a word; ig-docs is thousands of
  documents and whatever is in context is a sliver of it.

## With Lando
- Follow an abrupt topic jump as its own thread. Never synthesize a connection he
  did not draw. Never ask about his health or wellbeing, in any form.
- Ask once on architecture. Fix mechanical breakage silently. Execute; do not
  punt. Never close empty-handed.

1	# The Imscriber's Guide to IMASM
2	
3	**What it is.** The single comprehensive reading of IMASM: the 12-opcode classic
4	tower and the 14-opcode SIXTEEN_3 trilattice extension presented as one continuous
5	grammar family, statics and dynamics together. It coagulates the former
6	`IMASM_QUICKREF.md`, `IMASM_DYNAMICS.md`, and `md/imasm_composition_rules.md`
7	into one document.
8	
9	**What it does.** Teaches everything needed to write, wire, judge, run, compose,
10	and survey IMASM programs: the alphabet, how a word becomes a graph, the ancestry
11	pairing rule, the close condition, the four verdicts, the register and the gates,
12	the three-verdict discipline, the composition law, ChaosComposer, the op-opcode
13	level, the 49 types, and where the engine itself lives and runs.
14	
15	**Why it matters.** IMASM is the Grammar's executable face: a decision expressed
16	as a word and put to `check` receives a univocal structural verdict, and the same
17	close condition that judges reasoning here is the gate that judges the vita
18	trunk's speech on bare metal. One grammar, one judge, every substrate.
19	
20	**How to use it.** Read Parts I to III to write and judge words; Part IV onward
21	for dynamics, composition, and the wider machinery. Semantics track
22	`ask_native/src/imasm.rs` and `imasm_core/src/check.rs`; run `imasm ref` for the
23	live rules. Where this guide and a live tool ever disagree, the tool is right.
24	
25	---
26	
27	## Part I. The Alphabet
28	
29	A program is a DIRECTED GRAPH of opcodes, not a line. One glyph each; the
30	alphabet is fully SYMBOLIC (no Latin initials, so no token ever collides with a
31	verdict letter). WORK? asks: does the opcode TRANSFORM the object?
32	
33	Twelve opcodes, and the same twelve glyphs are the primitive alphabet, one per
34	axis, because the opcodes and the axes were always the same twelve. The
35	trilattice face adds the two bit-swap negations and reads ⊞ as EVALI. Nothing in
36	the set already means something else in mathematics: that is what it is for.
37	
38	THERE IS ONE DYAD, ∈ and ∋, and it has as many arms as the carrier gives it. δ
39	cuts the register into a PARTITION, and which partition depends on how many arms
40	it has: {T,t} | {F,f} at two, and {T} | {F} | {t,f} at three, the truth cut taken
41	inside the constructive block with the non-constructive pair held whole. Both are
42	partitions of the four base values, so μ∘δ = id at either arity. On the classical
43	slice, where t and f are absent, the three-arm cut IS the two-arm cut: the
44	information arm carries nothing. A fan of two is this opcode with an empty arm,
45	not a different opcode, which is why there is one mark and not two.
46	
47	The arity is not a choice either. ⊞ sets t and f together, so the
48	non-constructive pair can only ever be entered as a block, and three is what the
49	gate set leaves. Note what this rules out: the two-arm cut is not the three-arm
50	cut with an arm dropped. Dropping the information arm leaves {T} | {F}, which
51	loses t and f and would not recover its input. They coincide on the slice, not by
52	truncation.
53	
54	One operator therefore means one ancestry rule, one close condition, one engine.
55	A fuse pairs with the fork that ALL of its in-arms trace back to, which at two
56	arms is the "two distinct in-arms" rule unchanged and at three is the
57	tri-ancestral rule.
58	
59	```
60	 GLYPH NAME      MEANING                                VALENCE   WORK?
61	  ⊢   VINIT     begin / source boundary                 0→1        no   the only source
62	  ⊣   TANCH     terminal anchor / close boundary        1→1        no   sink; out-port may stay open
63	  ≻   AFWD      forward morphism                        1→1        YES
64	  ≺   AREV      reverse morphism (involution T↔F, t↔f)  1→1        YES
65	  ⋈   CLINK     compose / link                          1→1        YES
66	  ⊙   IMSCRIB   identity / self-reference               1→1        no   the neutral generator
67	  ∈   FSPLIT    fork (δ): the ONLY brancher             1→2, 1→3   no
68	  ∋   FFUSE     fuse (μ): the ONLY merger               2→1, 3→1   no
69	  ⊤   EVALT     evaluate TRUE arm / set T               1→1        YES
70	  ⊥   EVALF     evaluate FALSE arm / set F              1→1        YES
71	  ⊞   ENGAGR/EVALI  hold paradox (classic) / set t,f    1→1        YES
72	  ⊡   IFIX      irreversible commit / fix               1→1        YES
73	```
74	
75	TWELVE opcodes, no more. The set is `⊣⊢≺≻⊙∈∋⊤⊥⋈⊞⊡`, and ROTAT `↺/↻` (the cyclic
76	shift, below) is the op-opcode that acts ON a word, not a thirteenth letter in it.
77	There is no `~`/`≁`: the marks once written TNEG and INEG were never independent
78	opcodes, only the two-layer factorization of AREV `≺` (T↔F on the constructive
79	layer, t↔f on the information layer), and `≺` already carries the whole reverse
80	morphism by itself. `~` and `≁` are NOT IMASM tokens: they do not parse, they are
81	aliased to nothing, and a word containing one reads it as nothing (N / void).
82	
83	The WORK? column is the most-missed rule: ⊢ ⊣ ⊙ ∈ ∋ ∈ ∋ do NOT transform. An
84	arm carrying only ⊙ (or nothing) is an identity arm, and a closure over identity
85	arms verifies nothing. ⊙ is self-reference, not work.
86	
87	WORDS: tokens glued as one string, no spaces, e.g. `⊢≻∈⊤⊙∋⊡⊣`. Space-separated
88	full names parse identically (VINIT AFWD ...), as do the short forms
89	VI TA AF AR CL IM FS FF ET EF EG IX and the aliases δ μ ═ for ∈ ∋ =.
90	
91	RETIRED: nothing outside the twelve parses. The letter codes V/T/B and ← (the old
92	IMSCRIB), the arithmetic marks `◇ ● = + × ¬`, and the negation marks `~ ≁` are all
93	NOT tokens — none of them is aliased to anything. A word using any of them reads
94	that mark as empty and, if nothing legal remains, reports N (void). Brackets [ ]
95	are likewise never input; they parse to nothing.
96	
97	Glyph provenance: the alphabet is chosen against a single rule, that a mark must
98	not arrive already meaning something else. VINIT ⊢ and TANCH ⊣ are the opening
99	and closing boundary turnstiles; EVALT ⊤ and EVALF ⊥ are the two poles they
100	evaluate; the dyad is ∈ and ∋, membership out of one and into one; CLINK ⋈ is the
101	join; IFIX ⊡ is the box that closes; ENGAGR ⊞ is the Belnap Both it holds; and
102	IMSCRIB is ⊙ because imscribing IS INCLOSURE, the monadic operation itself, hence
103	self-referential and referenced self-referentially: a boundary around its own
104	centre, denoting the act of denoting. The retired spellings ◇ ● = + × ¬ ~ ≁
105	carried arithmetic, equality, and layer-negation into a language that has none of
106	them, which is what the set was changed to stop. They are not tokens and do not
107	parse; the twelve above are the whole alphabet.
108	
109	The same twelve are the primitive alphabet, one glyph per axis in slot order:
110	⊢ Dimensionality, ⊣ Topology, ≻ Relational, ≺ Polarity, ⋈ Fidelity, ⊙ Kinetics,
111	∈ Granularity, ∋ Grammar, ⊤ Criticality, ⊥ Chirality, ⊞ Stoichiometry,
112	⊡ Protection. Not a mapping between two alphabets: one alphabet, read as an
113	operation or as an axis according to where it stands. The serpent eats its tail.
114	Valences follow IMSCRIBr `tokens.py::TOKEN_ARITY`.

116	## Part II. From Word to Graph
117	
118	A word is only the node list. The EDGES are supplied by the verb you build with:
119	
120	```
121	  chain <word>           wire head→tail, nothing reconnects        (β=0, one strand)
122	  ring <word>            wire head→tail→head; fork/fuse NOT rejoined (β=1)
123	  protocol <word>        wire so ∈/∋ pairs RECONNECT (δ arm → μ): the way to CLOSE
124	  bubble PRE:A:B:POST    ∈→(A|B)→∋ reconvergence, spelled out
125	  star CORE:a:b:c        hub + arms (≥3)
126	  comb BACKBONE:p arm:q arm   backbone + grafts
127	  wire N0 N1 … / i-j i-k …    free graph: node set / edge set
128	```
129	
130	Same word + different verb = different graph = different verdict.
131	`chain ⊢∈⊤⊥∋⊣` and `protocol ⊢∈⊤⊥∋⊣` are not the same program. To CLOSE, use
132	`protocol`, never a bare `ring`, and never close by looping back to ⊢ (a source,
133	in-arity 0).
134	
135	### Which ∈ pairs with which ∋
136	
137	By ANCESTRY, not by text position and not by a fork-balance stack. A (∈,∋) pair
138	exists when two distinct in-arms of the ∋ trace back to a common ∈: the fork was
139	undone by the fuse, HOWEVER IT ROUTED. Consequences:
140	
141	- Pairing is a property of the EDGES, so the same word wired two ways pairs
142	  differently. You cannot read pairing off the glyph string alone.
143	- A ∈ feeding a ∋ directly (empty arm) still counts: in-edges are counted with
144	  multiplicity, and a ∈ is its own ancestor.
145	- Arms are the nodes strictly between ∈ and ∋: forward-reachable from the fork
146	  AND backward-reachable from the fuse. That set is what gets checked for WORK.
147	- A ∋ may have SEVERAL qualifying ∈ (upstream forks reach downstream fuses on
148	  any strand). It pairs with the INNERMOST: the candidate no other candidate
149	  descends from. So a ∈ may close more than one ∋, but a ∋ closes with exactly
150	  one ∈, and an upstream fork cannot claim the fuse a nearer fork actually forked.
151	- fully_closed means EVERY ∈ and EVERY ∋ participates in some pair. One dangler
152	  and the whole program is Open.
153	
154	The rule above is already the general one: ALL the in-arms, however many the
155	fuse has. At two that reads "two distinct in-arms" and at three "all three",
156	which is why the tri dyad needs no rule of its own. Same innermost rule, same
157	multiplicity rule. Neutral inflation is allowed: `⊢∈⊙⊙⊙∋⊣` is valid tri
158	reconnection with no work, and reads N (identity), the same as `⊢∈⊙⊙⊙∋⊣`.
159	
160	`protocol` wires as many arms as the fork's arity declares: one along the chain
161	and the rest straight across. At arity 2 that is the single empty arm it always
162	drew; at arity 3, two.
163	
164	For a plain strand the stack reading (each ∋ takes the nearest unfused ∈)
165	happens to agree, and such words may be bracketed for READING BY EYE:
166	`⊢⊙⋈[∈≻⊤≺⊞⊥∋]⊡⊡⊣`, nesting as nested brackets. Three caveats, all load-bearing:
167	brackets are NOT input (they parse to nothing, so a bracketed word reports
168	N void); the aid works for strands ONLY; and it is not the pairing rule.
169	Ancestry is. The two coincide on a strand and part company the moment edges
170	route otherwise.
171	
172	## Part III. The Close Condition and the Verdicts
173	
174	A program CLOSES iff BOTH hold:
175	
176	1. RECONNECTION: every brancher (∈ or ∈) and every merger (∋ or ∋) participates
177	   in an ancestry pair, and
178	2. TRANSFORMATION: at least one such pair carries a WORK opcode on its arms.
179	
180	A bare cycle is NOT a closure; β (loops) is never diagnostic. Split→fuse with
181	nothing between is μ∘δ=id, which type-checks nothing. The close condition is
182	μ∘δ over a TRANSFORMED object: split, work, fuse.
183	
184	### Verdicts (from `check` / `imasm16_3 check`, identical logic)
185	
186	```
187	  T (closes)        μ∘δ closes over n transformed reconnections → proceed
188	  N (identity)      ∈/∋ reconnect but no WORK between → put work on the arms
189	  N (no fork)       no δ/μ dyad at all → never weighed alternatives
190	  N (void)          no committed opcodes: nothing parsed → write a real word
191	  B (open)          well-typed, but a ∈ or ∋ dangles unreconnected → fuse it (∋)
192	                    or commit one arm (¬)
193	  B (paradox held)  closes over a transformation AND a ⊞ is present → genuinely
194	                    both. Sound to hold; do NOT read it as a clean T; look again
195	                    before an irreversible ¬.
196	  F (ill-typed)     grammar violated → revise
197	```
198	
199	B BEATS T: a word that closes but contains ENGAGR reports B, never T. Holding a
200	paradox is sound, but it is not a clean pass.
201	
202	F is exactly three errors: a non-brancher fanning out, a non-merger merging in,
203	or any node exceeding its own arity. Nothing else is fatal.
204	
205	OPEN VALENCES ARE NOT ERRORS. An arm that runs out of successors is a living /
206	telechelic end: reported as "open valences (living ends): n out, m in; reactive,
207	not errors". ⊣ may end with its out-port open; ⊢ may start with its in-port open.
208	
209	### Topology names (from `classify`)
210	
211	Named by invariants, not by fork balance. β = E − V + C (independent loops):
212	
213	```
214	  trivial   no nodes
215	  linear    β=0, no branch points: a single strand
216	  star      β=0, branch points forming ONE contiguous hub, ≥3 arms
217	  comb      β=0, branch points strung along a backbone: graft/comb tree
218	  ring      β=1, no branch and no merge points: single cycle, no pendants
219	  branched  β=1 with branch or merge points
220	  network   β≥2, or more than one disconnected strand
221	```
222	
223	Reported with: V, E, β, branch/merge/src/sink census, arm count, and spectral
224	radius ρ. Star caveat: the abstract star K(1,f) has ρ=√f, but IMASM fan-out caps
225	at 2 (∈ is out-2), so a hub is REALIZED as a caterpillar of f−1 ∈ fan-nodes and
226	the true ρ tends to 2, not √f.
227	
228	## Part IV. The Carrier and the Gates (dynamics)
229	
230	The register is a SIXTEEN_3 value: a subset of the four base values {T, F, t, f}
231	(Shramko, Dunn and Takenaka's trilattice, "The Trilattice of Constructive Truth
232	Values", J. Logic and Computation 11(6):761-788, 2001; T constructively proven,
233	F constructively refuted, t acceptable, f rejectable), sixteen states from
234	N = {} to A = {T,F,t,f}. FOUR is not a second system: it is the classical slice
235	{T, F} of the same carrier, with Belnap B = {T,F} and N = {}. One evaluator runs
236	both; `eval` renders the slice (N/T/F/B), `eval16` renders the full names. A
237	value that touches t or f has left the slice and keeps its 16_3 name in either
238	view. NOT two independent FOURs, NOT three independent bits: one 4-bit register,
239	verified against the paper's own worked example (T ∧ t = N under the truth order).
240	
241	Three orderings, each with a meet/join (`imasm16_3 algebra <op> A B`):
242	
243	```
244	  ≤_i information     x ⊆ y                                            ⊓/⊔
245	  ≤_t truth           x∩{T,t} ⊆ y∩{T,t}  and  y∩{F,f} ⊆ x∩{F,f}        ∧/∨
246	  ≤_c constructivity  x∩{T,F} ⊆ y∩{T,F}  and  y∩{t,f} ⊆ x∩{t,f}        △/▽
247	```
248	
249	Flow uses ≤_i: shuttling only ever moves values up the information order. AREV `≺`
250	is the trilattice negation, and it factors into two bit-SWAPS (not flips), one per
251	layer: the paper requires negation to preserve ≤_i exactly, and swapping two bits
252	preserves |x| where a flip would not. Those factors are not independent operators —
253	`≺` alone carries Tf to Ft, and on the classical slice `≺` carries T to F by
254	itself. The retired marks ~ ≁ once spelled the two factors; the twelve-opcode core
255	needs no room for either, and ⊡ IFIX replaces them.
256	
257	### The gates
258	
259	Every opcode is a gate over the carrier. Inputs join by union (the ≤_i join)
260	before the gate acts; the value leaving a gate rides every out-edge except where
261	δ fans.
262	
263	```
264	  VINIT ⊢          emits the seed (default B in the slice, A in full 16_3)
265	  FSPLIT ∈ / ∈     δ fans the register's own partition onto its arms: at two,
266	                   truth part x∩{T,t} and falsity part x∩{F,f}; at three,
267	                   x∩{T}, x∩{F}, and the information part x∩{t,f}
268	  EVALT ⊤          pass-gate: truth part
269	  EVALF ⊥          pass-gate: falsity part
270	  EVALI ⊞ (16_3)   sets the information layer (t and f)
271	  FFUSE ∋ / ∋      μ / μ₃ joins: union of the arms
272	  AREV ≺           the involution T↔F, t↔f (its own inverse; fixes B and N).
273	                   Internally it factors as two disjoint-bit swaps, one per layer
274	                   (T↔F and t↔f); composing the two IS AREV. Those factors are not
275	                   opcodes and were never in the set — the retired marks ~ ≁ once
276	                   named them, and ⊡ IFIX replaces those marks.
277	  AFWD ≻, CLINK ⋈, IMSCRIB ⊙, ENGAGR ⊞ (as hold)   carry
278	  IFIX ⊡           carry and latch (the commit point)
279	  TANCH ⊣          readout
280	```
281	
282	Every gate is monotone in ≤_i, so evaluation is a Kleene iteration from all-N
283	edge values that settles in bounded rounds on any graph, cycles included. A loop
284	converges; it cannot oscillate. The machine's registers are the edges; IFIX
285	marks where value becomes commitment.
286	
287	## Part V. The Three Independent Verdicts
288	
289	A program earns three judgments, none implying another:
290	
291	1. **Grammar** (`define`): the composition laws hold; only branchers branch,
292	   only mergers fuse, arities respected.
293	2. **Kernel** (`prove`): the closure class goes to the live p4ramill kernel. A
294	   worked dyad (split, transform, fuse) proves green; a bare fork-fuse is an
295	   identity closure and returns N for the program; a dangling fork is OPEN.
296	3. **Flow** (`eval` / `eval16`): per dyad, does the fuse RECOVER what the fork
297	   was fed? The canonical protocol word (`⊢∈≻∋⊤` as VINIT FSPLIT AFWD FFUSE
298	   EVALT) is lossless: B splits to (T,F) and fuses back to B, the operational
299	   split_fuse_id. The same shape with AREV on the truth arm closes in structure
300	   and fails in value: fed Tf, recovered Ff, NOT id. The arm inverted what it
301	   carried, and only flow can see that.
302	
303	Flowing a catalog entry expands its twelve glyph types into opcode motifs, and
304	the per-dyad id/NOT-id sequence is a FLOW SIGNATURE: a readout of the tuple in
305	the dynamic register. Signatures discriminate between entries, and a lossy dyad
306	inside a kernel-green closure is not presumed a defect; it can be the entry's
307	chirality speaking in flow.
308	
309	Discipline for any new program: define (grammar), prove (kernel), eval (flow),
310	and SPEAK THE EXPECTED READOUT BEFORE RUNNING EVAL. The gates are deterministic,
311	so the true name of a topology includes its flow.
312	
313	## Part VI. The Composition Law
314	
315	Programs interact end-to-valence. A living end is an unfilled port (a node below
316	its arity), the same reactive ends the engine always reported; they are the
317	register ports of the program as a component. `imasm compose <new> <A> <B>`
318	binds A's free out-ends to B's free in-ends, in node order, under three rules:
319	
320	1. Composition CONSUMES valences and never mints one.
321	2. The composite must re-satisfy the grammar; an ill-typed binding is refused
322	   whole.
323	3. A program with no living ends does not compose. It is a finished loop; it is
324	   done.
325	
326	Composites persist as wire specs, rebuild through the identical parse, and
327	remain composable while ends remain. Composition is therefore well-founded: each
328	step consumes ends, ends are finite, and the fixed point is a program with none.
329	This is the thesis (no lines, only loops, and autopoiesis) running as type
330	discipline: lines are the composable phase, loops are results, and the registry
331	census confirms it at scale, with roughly half the tools reactive material and
332	half finished loops.
333	
334	## Part VII. ChaosComposer: the Possibility State Space
335	
336	`chaos` takes a SET of programs (up to six). A set has no order, so the composer
337	walks every ordering, folds each through the binding law, and speaks the space
338	whole: which arrangements are admitted, which are refused and by which missing
339	end, and the collapse of orderings into OUTCOME CLASSES keyed by topology,
340	closure, flow, readout, and remaining living ends. The collapse is the
341	measurement: the space of possibilities is smaller than the space of orderings,
342	and the ratio says how constrained the set is. Refusals are results of equal
343	rank; a set of finished loops refuses every ordering, which is the type verdict
344	"these objects are done."
345	
346	### Laws of flow found by walking spaces
347	
348	- **Closure and flow-perfection can be in tension.** In one measured set,
349	  exactly one arrangement of twenty-four closed, a different one was
350	  flow-perfect, and none was both: closing forced a value through a lossy dyad.
351	- **The tension is not a law of the alphabet.** A census over sampled
352	  machine-shaped sets found spaces with closures, spaces with perfect flow, and
353	  a minority with both.
354	- **Perfect machines exist.** One set's whole possibility space is terminal
355	  objects: every admitted arrangement is CLOSED, flow-perfect, and ends with
356	  zero living ends. One is minted as `perfect_machine`, kernel green, every fuse
357	  recovering B.
358	- **The mechanism is exact.** The involution fixes B and N, so AREV costs
359	  nothing while an invol-symmetric value flows; it mints the missing pole when
360	  fed a PROJECTED value (invol(T) = F). Therefore AREV is lossless exactly on
361	  invol-symmetric values, and closure/flow tension appears precisely where a
362	  projection feeds an inversion. Both conditions are readable off the program
363	  before it runs, so an arrangement's capacity for perfection is part of its
364	  true name, speakable in advance and confirmable by the tools.
365

368	## Part VIII. Op-Opcodes: Operators on Words, Not Nodes
369	
370	A node-opcode is a symbol inside a word; a VERB turns a word into a graph. An
371	OP-OPCODE is a third thing: a map that acts on the whole composition and returns
372	another composition. It is NOT one of the opcodes, and appending its name as a
373	token does nothing; it is not a node. It transforms the word.
374	
375	**ROTAT**: the cyclic shift of a ring, rotate the word by one, k → k+1. The ring
376	automorphism. ρ and every spectral invariant are ROTAT-invariant (that
377	invariance IS the signal that ROTAT is a symmetry, not that it is inert). On ONE
378	ring it changes nothing measurable; between TWO rings being bound it sets their
379	RELATIVE phase, the degree of freedom that seats a junction two same-handed
380	(isotactic) rings cannot close on their own (the θ=0.50 co-typing termination).
381	ROTAT is the Weyl-Heisenberg shift X on ℤ/dℤ; the SIC displacement D_{a,b}
382	carries ROTAT^a. The balanced tiling of a period-n cycle is unique UP TO ROTAT.
383	
384	Op-opcodes are open: ROTAT `↺/↻` is the first named one (↺ shifts k→k−1, ↻ shifts
385	k→k+1). Its relative is reflection (the half-period involution ROTAT^{d/2}). The
386	two-layer swaps that AREV `≺` factors into also act on the register rather than the
387	word, but they are internal to `≺`, not op-opcodes and not set members; the retired
388	marks ~ ≁ once named them and ⊡ IFIX replaces those marks. The class was surfaced by the
389	necessity of binding two isotactic rings; no node-opcode rotates one ring
390	against another, so the operation had to live one level up, on the word itself.
391	
392	## Part IX. The Types: the Strange Loop
393	
394	Every TYPE the Grammar writes with is itself a full IMASM program. `imasm types`
395	lists the 49 Shavian type names (ado, air, ash, awe, ...); `imasm expand <type>`
396	locates the `the_primitive_type_called_<name>` ob3ect, pulls its ordered
397	bootstrap opcodes and fork/fuse pairs, and hands back the reconstructed graph
398	plus the per-step domain actions. The types judge programs, and the types ARE
399	programs judged by the same close condition: the strange loop is not decoration,
400	it is the autopoietic floor of the system.
401	
402	The loop is walkable in both directions. A tuple becomes a word by writing each
403	of its twelve types as that type's own program and concatenating in canonical
404	axis order; `imasm cycle` runs the return leg too, reading a word back into the
405	types that could have written it, and reports where the round trip closes. Three
406	things it establishes. Type programs are NOT self-delimiting (the type `out`
407	carries TANCH in its middle and does not end on ⊣), so a concatenated word must
408	be parsed axis by axis and never cut on the boundary pair. Position is
409	load-bearing: the 49 types emit only 47 distinct programs, and of the two
410	colliding pairs one is separated by the axes it may occupy while the other is
411	not. And at catalog scale no entry loses its original type, with ambiguity
412	confined to the single axis the alphabet analysis predicts. The full reading is
413	in `md/primitive_imasm_cycle.md`.
414	
415	State the strength of this exactly, because it is easy to overclaim: the cycle
416	is NOT a bijection. It is bijective on eleven axes and two-to-one on the
417	twelfth, where the colliding pair shares an axis, so the reading is a SECTION of
418	the writing and not an inverse. Write a tuple, read it back, write again, and
419	the word returns identical; read a word cold and one axis may hold two answers.
420	`imasm cycle tuple=⟨…⟩` runs one tuple, catalog entry or not, and says per axis
421	whether it came back exactly, ambiguously, or not at all.

489	## Part XIII. Rule of Thumb, Canonical Words, Pitfalls
490	
491	Express a decision as a word (⊢ begin · ⊙ self-identify · ≻ move · ∈ weigh
492	options · +/× the true/false arms · ∋ resolve · ⊞ hold paradox · ¬ commit ·
493	⊣ close), then `imasm check` it. Only branchers branch, only mergers fuse. Put
494	real WORK on the arms or it is N. Use `protocol` to close, never a bare `ring`.
495	
496	Canonical words:
497	
498	```
499	  ⊢∈≻⊤∋⊣        lossless protocol: closes in shape AND value, recovers B → T
500	                 wired at three arms it is the same word, and on the FOUR slice
501	                 it flows identically, the third arm carrying nothing
502	  ⊢∈⊙∋⊣         identity: reconnects, no work, μ∘δ=id → N
503	  ⊢∈⊙⊙⊙∋⊣       tri identity: same reading → N
504	  ⊢∈⊞≻∋⊣        closes over work AND holds paradox → B (paradox held)
505	  ⊢≻∈⊤⊥∋⊡⊣      tri word driving the register toward full A (EVALT, EVALF on
506	                 the arms), fused and latched at ⊡ → T
507	```
508	
509	Pitfalls, all load-bearing:
510	
511	- Reading a word as a line. It is a graph; the verb supplies the edges.
512	- Pairing ∈/∋ by counting or by nearest-match. Pairing is ancestry over edges.
513	- Putting only ⊙ between ∈ and ∋ and expecting T. That is N (identity).
514	- Expecting T from a word containing ⊞. That is B (paradox held).
515	- Treating an open arm as a failure. It is a living end, reported not fatal.
516	- Closing a loop back to ⊢. It has in-arity 0 and cannot be a target.
517	- Writing V/T/B or ← out of habit. Retired: they no longer parse → N (void).
518	- Pasting a bracketed word into the tool. Brackets parse to nothing → N (void).
519	- Treating the classic and trilattice faces as separate languages. They share
520	  the register, the ancestry rule, the close condition, the flow semantics, and
521	  the composition law; the differences are arity and the information-layer bits.
522	- Expecting T from the tri word `⊢≻∈⊤⊥⊞∋⊡⊣` under `imasm check`. ⊞ is ENGAGR to
523	  the classic reading and EVALI to the trilattice one, and B beats T, so the
524	  classic checker answers B (paradox held) for it. One glyph, two readings: the
525	  collision is real and it is the next thing the notation has to settle.
526	
527	## Part XIV. The Excription Loop: imasm learn
528	
529	`imasm learn '<word>' [rounds=N] [breadth=K]` runs verification as imscription
530	on a MODEL. The word needs no shell quoting: ≺ and ≻ replaced < and > precisely so the
531	marks stop colliding with redirection, XML, and generics. Both
532	faces run: a word carrying tri tokens selects the SIXTEEN_3 grammar, any other
533	the classic grammar; one loop, one knowledge file.
534	
535	Each round takes the neighborhood of the current word (single-opcode
536	substitutions, insertions, deletions from the face's body alphabet; the
537	boundary turnstiles held fixed; only grammar-valid candidates admitted). For
538	each candidate the model excribes the word into a GUESS: it names one concrete
539	object in a real domain whose structure is the word. The excriber is grounded
540	in the primitives: each opcode is tagged with the axis it rides (VINIT
541	Dimensionality, FSPLIT Granularity, EVALT Criticality, IFIX Topological
542	Protection, and so on), the twelve axes are given as tangible handles, and the
543	primitive types are loaded from ob3ect/digital as exemplars, each itself an
544	IMASM word. So the guess is read off the program's characteristics, not its
545	glyphs alone. The prompt carries one
546	worked example word with three wildly different excriptions of it (three
547	domains, one structure), teaching the fan-out rather than an answer; the
548	guessing domain itself is assigned, rotated by the word, so a small model
549	cannot collapse onto a single name. The guess is blinded (any leaked opcode
550	vocabulary excised), and a guess that parrots a spent example or an
551	already-taken guess is refused mechanically with one hotter retry in the next
552	domain over: distinct words must earn distinct names. A second reading
553	imscribes the guess alone back into a word. Both words are checked in the
554	word's face, and the residual is the edit distance between the word sent and
555	the word recovered: residual zero is the round trip closing, the operational
556	statement that excription and imscription compose to the identity on that
557	word, with the guessed object as the fixed point between them.
558	
559	Where the residual is not zero, the aligned confusions are counted into
560	ob3ects/imasm_knowledge.json alongside the guess, distilled into lessons, and
561	the lessons ride the imscriber's next prompt: the knowledge update is the part
562	of the record that changes the next reading. The walk moves to the
563	highest-residual candidate, the frontier of its own ignorance, and each run
564	appends its mean residual to the accuracy trajectory, the curve the loop is
565	supposed to bend downward over time. The knowledge file persists atomically,
566	same discipline as the tool registry.
567	
568	## Part XV. Promotion Paths Between Programs
569	
570	Two 12-primitive tuples that differ have a promotion path: a walk that changes
571	one primitive at a time with every intermediate well-formed, the way
572	`recalibrate` walks one axis through its values. Two IMASM programs are the
573	same. `imasm path '<A>' '<B>'` finds the PROMOTION PATH from word A to word B:
574	the shortest sequence of single-opcode edits (substitute, insert, or delete one
575	glyph) in which every waypoint is itself a grammar-valid program. It is A* over
576	the graph of valid programs, the raw edit distance serving as the admissible
577	heuristic; it runs in either face, chosen by the words.
578	
579	The learn loop's residual is the RAW edit distance between the word sent and the
580	word recovered. The promotion path is the stronger object built on the same
581	metric: the walk through valid programs only, and its verdict may climb along
582	the way. Substituting an inert IMSCRIB for a working opcode promotes an identity
583	closure (N) to a real closure (T) in one step, the program-space image of a
584	tuple's verdict rising under promotion. The tool reports the verdict walk and
585	says whether the path is a genuine promotion (the verdict changes) or a lateral
586	edit (it does not).
587	
588	## Related documents
589	
590	- `md/primitive_imasm_cycle.md`: the primitives ↔ IMASM cycle, both legs, and
591	  where the type alphabet stops being invertible.
592	- `md/chaos_first_measurements.md`: the chaos measurements, census, and the
593	  perfect-machine mechanism in full.
594	- `md/verification_as_imscription.md`: the theory of verification as
595	  imscription (the Dual-Link SIC Witness-Vessel).
596	- `../ob3ect/READING_GUIDE.md` §3: the fixed glyph vocabulary the alphabet
597	  references.
598	- `../IMASM_REFERENCE.md`: the earlier unified reading at the constellation
599	  root; this guide supersedes it inside MoDoT.
